L6: # Initial Management of Superior Vena Cava Obstruction
L7: ## Introduction
L8: 
L9: Superior Vena Cava Obstruction (SVCO) is an oncological emergency and any patients should be discussed with a Registrar or above immediately, and with the local Respiratory team or on-call Oncology team at the Beatson (【3†Appendix 6】 for contact details), as soon as possible to guide investigation and management.
L10: SVCO results from the compression of the superior vena cava by either a tumour arising in the right main or upper lobe bronchus or mediastinal lymphadenopathy. Initially it is diagnosed clinically in the presence of neck and facial swelling and distended veins over the anterior chest wall. There may also be swelling of one or both arms and symptoms of dyspnoea and headache. Malignancy is the commonest cause (>90%), most typically lung cancer, lymphoma, metastatic disease, mesothelioma and thymoma.
L11: Where relevant, the West of Scotland guideline on the '【4†Management of Newly Presenting Patients with a Mediastinal Mass Causing Airway Compromise†rightdecisions.scot.nhs.uk】' may be helpful.
L12: ## Assessment / monitoring
L13: 
L14: Obtain full history including:
L15: 
L16:   * Details of known malignancies and their treatment.
L17:   * The development of new or worsening respiratory symptoms, arm swelling and headaches, and rapidity of onset.
L18:   * Co-morbidities
L19:   * Medication including use of and contraindications to corticosteroids and anticoagulation.
L20: 
L21: Examine for distended external and internal jugular veins, collateral veins on the anterior chest wall, facial, arm and neck swelling, and conjunctival redness.
L22: The investigation of choice is a contrast-enhanced venous phase CT thorax (+/- abdomen and pelvis) if first presentation +/- CT pulmonary angiogram (CTPA). This defines tumour extent, and often the site of occlusion or stenosis and the extent of any thrombus formation. Appropriate CT imaging should be discussed with the on call radiologist. Impending SVCO can be an incidental finding on CT.
L23: Confirmation of diagnosis by histology may involve fine needle aspirate of palpable nodes, bronchoscopy, or CT guided biopsy. Seek advice from Respiratory or Oncology as soon as possible to guide investigation and management.
L24: 
L25: In addition to above, questions that may influence whether the patient should be considered for SVC stent or chemotherapy / radiotherapy are:
L26:   * Is there a relative contraindication for radiotherapy? For example previous chest / mediastinal radiotherapy? Is the patient able to lie reasonably flat?
L27:   * What is the patient's performance status? (0=normal activity, 1=restricted daily activity, 2=ambulatory and self caring, out of bed >50% of the day, 3=capable of limited self care, in bed >50% time, 4=unable to self care, chair/bed-bound).
L28:   * Is stenting procedure available? (This is performed by interventional radiology.)
L29: ## Treatment / drug therapy
L30: Treatment is initially to alleviate symptoms and (when known) directed at the underlying cause. Ensure that the patient has no life-threatening symptoms (e.g. associated stridor) and is fit enough for active treatment. If no contraindication to corticosteroids, commence dexamethasone oral (IV if swallow problems) 8 mg twice daily (morning and lunchtime) with gastroprotection if appropriate (e.g.
L31: omeprazole oral 20mg daily or lansoprazole oral 30mg once daily). Dexamethasone may be commenced whilst waiting for CT if clinical suspicion of SVCO is high. If CT confirms SVCO continue dexamethasone and seek urgent advice. As symptoms improve, dose may be gradually reduced over several weeks. If symptoms do not improve after 7 days consider stopping. If the CT scan shows no SVCO, then stop dexamethasone.
L32: Other treatments frequently used are radiotherapy, stent insertion and chemotherapy and will depend on clinical scenario. If thrombus is present, consider anticoagulation if no contraindications (see GGC guideline '【5†Treatment and Secondary Prophylaxis of Venous Thrombosis in Patients with Malignant Disease†rightdecisions.scot.nhs.uk】' for treatment options and considerations).

L66@P0: Introduction
L67@P0: La veine cave supérieure (VCS) est le principal vaisseau de retour veineux pour la tête,
L68@P0: la nuque, les membres supérieurs et la région
L69@P0: thoracique supérieure (1).
L70@P0: Le syndrome de la veine cave supérieure
L71@P0: (SVCS) est un état pathologique résultant d’une
L72@P0: obstruction de la veine cave supérieure. Il peut
L73@P0: comporter des céphalées, une dyspnée ou des
L74@P0: douleurs thoraciques. En outre, des signes
L75@P0: cliniques tels un stridor, une toux ainsi qu’un
L76@P0: œdème du visage et des membres supérieurs
L77@P0: peuvent également être constatés, tout comme
L78@P0: une dilatation veineuse de la région nuchale et
L79@P0: thoracique (1, 2).
L80@P0: La principale étiologie d’un SVCS est une
L81@P0: compression ou une infiltration de la VCS par
L82@P0: une lésion tumorale. D’autres causes sont
L83@P0: également décrites comme un anévrisme, une
L84@P0: thrombose, un hygrome ou une médiastinite.
L85@P0: Un cathéter veineux central peut également
